interest: This file provides crucial insight into the economic deconcentration program of the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP) in occupied Japan, specifically highlighting the policy distinction between productive industrial firms and non-producing trading conglomerates. The transmittal despatch reveals internal SCAP reasoning from the Anti-trust and Cartels Division: while manufacturing zaibatsu affiliates were slated for reorganization, Mitsui and Mitsubishi Trading Companies were singled out for outright liquidation to prevent them from leveraging prewar foreign contacts and informal cartels to monopolize revived foreign trade at the expense of emerging small businesses. Moreover, the accompanying directive (SCAPIN 1741) demonstrates the meticulous legal mechanisms employed by Occupation authorities to prevent the surreptitious reconstitution of these monopolies, imposing stringent prohibitions against former executive association, collective re-employment of employee cohorts, and the reuse of corporate names or office premises.
keywords: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
overview: This file comprises Despatch No. 1163 from the Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan to the Department of State, transmitting SCAP directive SCAPIN 1741 (dated July 3, 1947) concerning the dissolution of the Mitsui Trading Company (Mitsui Bussan) and the Mitsubishi Trading Company (Mitsubishi Shoji). The transmittal despatch elucidates SCAP's economic deconcentration policy, explaining that while most restricted zaibatsu operating companies were to be reorganized rather than dismantled, these two massive trading entities were targeted for complete liquidation because they produced no physical goods and posed a threat of monopolizing Japanese foreign trade through their entrenched international cartel connections. The enclosed SCAP directive mandates immediate liquidation by the Japanese Holding Company Liquidation Commission (HCLC), freezing transactions, mandating asset inventories for open-market disposal, and imposing strict personnel and organizational restrictions to prevent former officers, branch managers, or large cohorts of employees from reconstituting monopolistic enterprises or reusing the company names and offices.

subfiles.summary: The United States Political Adviser for Japan transmits to the Department of State a copy of SCAPIN 1741, which orders the dissolution of the Mitsubishi Trading Company and the Mitsui Trading Company by the Japanese Holding Company Liquidation Commission. The despatch reports on discussions with the Chief of SCAP's Anti-trust and Cartels Division, who clarified that while most industrial zaibatsu concerns producing goods would be reorganized rather than liquidated, these two non-producing trading giants were targeted for outright dissolution. The measure was designed both to impel other restricted companies to submit reorganization plans and to prevent the two giant trading firms from using prewar cartel ties and foreign connections to corner postwar foreign commerce at the expense of independent Japanese manufacturers.

subfiles.about: SCAP directive ordering the Japanese Government to immediately commence the dissolution and liquidation of the Mitsubishi and Mitsui trading companies under HCLC supervision.
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (signed by Colonel R. M. Levy, Adjutant General)
subfiles.summary: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers issues directive SCAPIN 1741 instructing the Japanese Government to immediately begin the dissolution and liquidation of the Mitsubishi Trading Company and the Mitsui Trading Company. The memorandum prohibits both firms from carrying out business transactions or asset transfers without approval from the Holding Company Liquidation Commission (HCLC) and bars former officers, directors, branch managers, and section heads from establishing new enterprises together or having more than two employed by any single firm. It further restricts groups of over one hundred employees from joining or forming companies without HCLC clearance, forbids the reuse of corporate names and business premises, mandates asset inventories and open-market sales, and requires immediate compliance reports.
